title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough — batching & KV cache (cost model)
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Verdant Payments through Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix/KV cache with a simple cost model. Discussed current traffic profile, latency SLOs, data residency, and tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot benchmark and share security docs + pricing. Action items and next steps captured.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Omar and Noah from our Optimize team. Quick intro?
[00:08] Lena Torres: Hey, I'm Lena, Head of AI at Verdant Payments. Samir and Priya are here too.
[00:12] Samir Desai: Samir, platform engineering.
[00:14] Priya Nair: Priya, SRE.
[00:16] Maya Chen: Great. Today we'll walk through batching and prefix/KV caching recommendations and show the cost model — with an eye to your latency SLOs.
[00:28] Omar Patel: Quick agenda: measurement, batching patterns, KV/prefix cache, cost math, questions, then next steps.
[00:35] Ethan Cole: One ask up front — we need clear tradeoffs, like if we bump batching how much does p99 change, and how big a dedicated commit we'd need.
[00:45] Omar Patel: Totally. Before we start, can you share current traffic profile? average seq length?
[00:52] Samir Desai: We're at 120 requests/s peak, 35 tokens avg/response, 99th latency target 400ms for critical flows. Most calls are short chat completions, some long-form generation during reconciliation runs.
[01:06] Maya Chen: Good — that mix is fairly typical. For short responses batching helps throughput but can add queueing latency; prefix/KV cache helps when you have repeated prefixes or system prompts.
[01:20] Omar Patel: If you look at dynamic batching, Redwood can micro-batch requests up to a few hundred ms depending on your SLO. Example: at 120 rps, a 20ms batch window increases avg batch size to ~2.4 which reduces per-token GPU cost.
[01:35] Priya Nair: Sorry, when you say per-token GPU cost, is that measured as tokens/sec per GPU or $/token?
[01:40] Noah Rivera: We show both. The cost model converts GPU time to dollars using your reserved or hosted rates. So we estimate tokens/sec and multiply by unit price.
[01:48] Maya Chen: Let me pull up a quick chart — (screen share) — here's a sim: no batching vs 20ms vs 50ms windows. At your traffic, 20ms gives a ~18% cost reduction, 50ms ~30% but p99 increases ~60-90ms.
[02:05] Lena Torres: That p99 hit is concerning for payments flow.
[02:08] Omar Patel: Understood. We often recommend hybrid policies: strict latency routes (auth, payment confirm) use minimal or no batching, other non-critical routes can use larger batch windows. Redwood supports per-route policies.
[02:20] Samir Desai: Can we pin model variants for those routes?
[02:23] Maya Chen: Yes — you can route critical flows to a lower-latency model variant or a dedicated pool.
[02:28] Priya Nair: Tell us about the KV/prefix cache — we have a lot of repeated system prompts for risk checks.
[02:33] Omar Patel: Prefix or KV cache stores key-value activations for tokens of the prefix so for repeated prompts the runtime can reuse KV cache instead of recomputing. If you have high repetition, hit rates >60% drastically cut per-request compute.
[02:46] Noah Rivera: In the demo corpus we loaded, a 70% cache hit reduced token compute time by ~55% and cost by ~40% in the cost model. However, cache memory overhead increases, so you need cluster capacity planning.
[02:59] Lena Torres: Does caching affect data residency or PII concerns?
[03:03] Maya Chen: Good question. KV cache entries are transient and stored in memory; in Redwood Private you can ensure they never leave your VPC. We also have controls to scrub or avoid caching sensitive prompts.
[03:15] Priya Nair: For hosted, what's retention?
[03:18] Omar Patel: Hosted keeps caches ephemeral per instance and we do not persist to disk; but if you require stricter controls, Private deployment is recommended.
[03:26] Samir Desai: Walk us through an end-to-end cost example for our numbers.
[03:30] Noah Rivera: Sure — baseline: 120 rps * 35 tokens = 4200 tokens/sec. Using our cost table, on hosted mixed model that's ~X GPU-seconds -> $Y per hour. With 20ms batching, effective GPU secs drop 18%, so cost Y*(1-0.18). With 70% cache hit VM reduction, multiply again.
[03:49] Maya Chen: I'll be explicit in the follow-up spreadsheet, but rough ballpark: you could see 30-45% unit-cost reduction across non-critical workloads with combined batching+cache.
[03:59] Lena Torres: Are those savings sensitive to sequence length? We have reconciliation jobs that generate 1k tokens.
[04:05] Omar Patel: Yes — for long sequences batching has diminishing returns because the generation itself dominates GPU time; but KV cache helps when the prefix repeats across the long generation (less common). For long sequences, quantization and model selection matter more.
[04:20] Maya Chen: Quick note on dedicated pools: if you commit to a reserved capacity, your $/GPU is lower so the break-even for dedicated vs hosted depends on utilization. Our cost model will compute the commit size needed to hit your target unit economics.
[04:34] Samir Desai: We need guidance on commit sizing — we can't overcommit.
[04:38] Noah Rivera: We'll run a sensitivity analysis in the spreadsheet: utilization curves, break-even points for 50%, 70%, 90% utilization.
[04:46] Priya Nair: Any constraints for autoscaling? We need predictable latency spikes during peak capture windows.
[04:51] Omar Patel: Autoscaling can be configured to keep a small buffer of warm workers to meet p99 SLOs, and we support burst capacity. But again it's a cost vs latency tradeoff.
[05:03] Maya Chen: Moving to the demo — (screen share) Optimize console, batching tab.
[05:10] [screen share noise — brief pause]
[05:20] Omar Patel: Here you can set per-route batch windows, max batch size, and prioritize routes. This console also surfaces estimated cost delta and predicted p50/p95/p99 impact.
[05:34] Lena Torres: That predicted p99 looks optimistic — how accurate are these?
[05:38] Noah Rivera: Models are based on telemetry from similar workloads and your sampled traces if you share them. There is noise — we mark this as an estimate.
[05:46] Samir Desai: What telemetry would you need from us?
[05:49] Omar Patel: Sampled request traces with token counts, timestamps, and route labels — 24–72 hours of traffic helps. You can also run our benchmark harness inside your VPC for Private assessments.
[06:01] Priya Nair: OK. On security docs, we need SOC2 and encryption details.
[06:05] Maya Chen: We'll send the security pack after the call — SOC 2, ISO, SSO/SAML, RBAC docs, KMS options.
[06:11] Lena Torres: Great. Any competitors you recommend we benchmark against?
[06:15] Omar Patel: Common names we see mentioned are Anthropic, OpenAI (Managed), and self-hosted Triton stacks.
[06:23] Samir Desai: We'll definitely do a Triton bench internally.
[06:27] Maya Chen: Quick recap and recommended pilot: two-week pilot with Redwood Optimize — we'll run a benchmark using a sampled traffic set, evaluate batching windows 0/20/50ms, run KV cache with TTLs, and produce a sensitivity cost model and commit sizing.
[06:45] Ethan Cole: Timeline?
[06:47] Maya Chen: Start next Monday — 2 weeks — bench + report. Deliverables: benchmark results, spreadsheet, security pack, and pricing options.
[06:58] Lena Torres: Sounds good. A couple of clarifying q's: can we have an NDA add-on for the pilot?
[07:03] Maya Chen: Yes we can attach an NDA.
[07:06] Samir Desai: For the pilot, will Redwood provision a dedicated private env or can we run the harness against your hosted endpoints?
[07:12] Noah Rivera: We can do either. For the most realistic dedicated-sizing output we recommend running the harness in your VPC or our Private. If that's heavy, we can simulate via hosted endpoints but that may underreport some cache behavior.
[07:28] Priya Nair: Anything else?
[07:30] Maya Chen: I'll email the pilot plan, security docs and the spreadsheet. Omar will own the benchmark run, Noah will do the sensitivity analysis.
[07:38] Omar Patel: I'll get you the harness instructions.
[07:41] Lena Torres: Thanks everyone.
[07:43] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with next steps.
[07:45] [call ends]
